blocks.content: The previous chapter established that a program works with logical addresses while the hardware works with physical addresses, and that the Memory Management Unit sits in between translating one into the other. What that chapter left open is a timing question: exactly when does this translation get decided? The answer is not the same for every program on every system, and the choice made has real consequences for how flexible and how fast a program can be.

This chapter answers that timing question directly. There are exactly three distinct points in a program's life where the binding of a logical address to a physical address can happen: compile time, load time, and run time. Each one trades away a different amount of flexibility for a different amount of simplicity, and only one of the three is actually usable on a modern general purpose operating system.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408967926-146931144.png
1. The Core Question: When Does Binding Happen?
blocks.text: 1. The Core Question: When Does Binding Happen?

blocks.content: Address binding is the act of mapping a logical address a program uses onto the physical address it actually corresponds to in RAM. That mapping has to happen at some point before data can actually be read or written, but nothing forces it to happen at any particular stage of a program's life. It could be decided the moment the program is compiled, the moment it is loaded into memory, or continuously while it runs.

Each of these three moments is a genuinely different design choice, not just a technical detail. The earlier binding happens, the simpler the resulting hardware and software can be, but the less freedom the operating system has afterward to move the program around. The later binding happens, the more overhead is paid on every memory access, but the more freedom the system keeps for as long as the program is alive.

Understanding these three points by name, and being able to explain exactly what each one gains and gives up, is one of the most reliably asked foundational questions in operating systems interviews. The rest of this chapter walks through all three in order, from the earliest and most rigid to the latest and most flexible.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: Address binding is simply the question of when a logical address gets tied to a real physical address: at compile time, at load time, or continuously at run time.
2. Compile Time Binding

Compile time binding is the earliest possible point at which addresses can be decided. If the exact physical memory location a program will run at is already known in advance, before the program is even compiled, the compiler can generate absolute physical addresses directly into the compiled code. There is no offset to add later and no translation step to perform while the program runs, the addresses baked into the code are already the real physical addresses.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408967926-613979005.png

This sounds efficient, and in a narrow sense it is, but it requires a very strong guarantee: the operating system must be certain that this exact program will always load into this exact region of physical memory, every single time it runs, with no other program ever competing for that same region. On a modern multiprogrammed system running many processes at once, with memory being constantly allocated and freed, that guarantee is essentially never true.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408967926-334155074.png

{"headers":["Requirement for compile time binding","Why it is needed","True on modern general purpose systems"],"rows":[["Exact physical load address known in advance","The compiler has to bake the correct final address directly into the code","Rarely, memory layout is decided dynamically while the system runs"],["Physical region reserved for this program alone","No other process can be allowed to occupy that region instead","Rarely, general purpose systems run many competing processes at once"],["No relocation ever needed after compiling","There is no translation step left to adjust the address later","Rarely, processes are routinely moved, swapped, and reloaded"]]}

Because these three requirements are so rarely satisfied together, compile time binding survives mainly as a historical technique from early single program computers. Today it mostly shows up in small embedded systems that run exactly one permanently fixed program with no operating system managing multiple competing processes at all.
3. Load Time Binding

Load time binding relaxes the strict requirement compile time binding demands. The eventual physical location does not need to be known while the program is being compiled. Instead, the compiler generates relocatable addresses, offsets measured from an unknown starting point rather than fixed absolute values. The program is now portable to wherever it eventually ends up loading.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408967926-184934963.png

The actual final physical addresses only get computed once the program is about to run, right at the moment the loader places it into memory. The loader picks a real physical starting location, adds it to every relocatable offset the compiler produced, and from that point forward the program's addresses are fixed. This single binding step happens exactly once, right before execution begins, never again after that.

This is meaningfully more flexible than compile time binding, since the same compiled program can now load at a different physical address on different runs, or on different machines, without needing to be recompiled. But a real limitation remains: once the loader finishes binding addresses and the program starts executing, that program can never be moved to a different physical location again for the rest of its run.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408967926-649700983.png
4. Run Time Binding

Run time binding, also called execution time binding, pushes the decision all the way to the opposite extreme. Instead of binding addresses once, at compile time or at load time, the binding of logical to physical addresses is deferred until the program is actually running, and it happens fresh on every single memory access, not once and never again but continuously, for as long as the program executes.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408967927-981924826.png

This continuous translation is exactly what the Memory Management Unit performs, covered in full detail in the Logical vs Physical Address chapter that opens this module. The MMU sits between the CPU and RAM, and on every instruction fetch and every variable access it takes the logical address the program just generated and translates it into a physical address right then, using whatever mapping the operating system currently has in place.

The crucial consequence of this constant, per access translation is relocation. Run time binding is the only one of the three binding times that allows a process to be freely moved to a different physical location in RAM even after it has already started executing. Because the translation is redone on every access rather than fixed once, the operating system only has to update the mapping the MMU consults, and the very next memory access is translated correctly against the new location automatically.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408968438-682474250.png

blocks.title: Why this matters so much
blocks.content: Run time binding is the modern standard used by essentially every general purpose operating system today. It is slightly more expensive than the other two, since translation work happens on every single access rather than once, but the flexibility it buys, letting the operating system freely relocate, swap, and rearrange processes in physical memory while they are actively running, is considered well worth that cost.
5. Comparing All Three Binding Times

With all three explained individually, lining them up side by side makes the trade off pattern obvious: the later binding happens, the more freedom the operating system keeps, and the earlier binding happens, the simpler and cheaper the resulting execution becomes.

{"headers":["Binding time","When translation happens","Can the process be relocated after starting","Typical modern usage"],"rows":[["Compile time","Once, before the program is even compiled into its final form","No, never, the physical address is permanently fixed","Rare, mostly historical or tiny fixed purpose embedded systems"],["Load time","Once, right when the loader places the program into memory","No, the address is fixed the moment execution begins","Uncommon, seen in some simple loaders and small systems"],["Run time","Continuously, fresh on every single memory access, via the MMU","Yes, freely, at any point during execution","The modern standard on essentially every general purpose operating system"]]}

Notice that only run time binding answers yes to relocation after execution has started. That single difference is the reason nearly every modern operating system is built entirely around it, and it is the detail interviewers most often probe for when this topic comes up.
6. Why Paging and Virtual Memory Require Run Time Binding
blocks.text: 6. Why Paging and Virtual Memory Require Run Time Binding

blocks.content: Run time binding is not simply the more convenient of the three options, it is a hard requirement for paging and virtual memory to function at all. Both of those mechanisms, covered in their own dedicated chapters in this module, depend on a process's memory being split into pages that can live anywhere in physical RAM, not held together in one contiguous block the way compile time and load time binding both assume.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408968440-169932067.png
blocks.alt: Why Paging and Virtual Memory Require Run Time Binding

blocks.content: Under paging, the pages belonging to a single process are routinely scattered across non contiguous physical frames, and under demand paging a page can be evicted out of RAM entirely and, later, reloaded into a completely different frame than the one it originally occupied. A translation scheme that only bound addresses once, at load time, would have no way to represent this constantly shifting, per page mapping. Only run time binding, refreshed on every single access through the MMU's page table lookup, can correctly follow a mapping that keeps changing while the process is still running.

blocks.title: The connection to remember
blocks.content: Paging and virtual memory are only possible because run time binding already exists underneath them. Every page table lookup performed by the MMU on every memory access is run time binding in action, just applied at the granularity of individual pages instead of one single base register.
7. A Worked Example Across All Three
blocks.text: 7. A Worked Example Across All Three

blocks.content: Consider the exact same compiled program, and imagine it built and handled under each of the three binding strategies in turn, to make the difference between them completely concrete rather than abstract.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408968440-197481003.png
blocks.alt: A Worked Example Across All Three

blocks.content: Under compile time binding, the compiler is told the program will always load at physical address 5000, and it bakes that number directly into the compiled instructions. The program will only ever run correctly if it lands at exactly physical address 5000, every single time, on every machine it is ever deployed to. There is zero room to place it anywhere else without recompiling from scratch.

Under load time binding, the same source code is compiled into relocatable offsets instead, with no physical address assumed yet. When the loader eventually runs this program, it might place it at physical address 5000 this time and physical address 20000 the next time, and either way the loader computes and fixes the final addresses once, right there, before execution starts. Flexibility has improved: the program can now load anywhere, but once it starts running, it is stuck at whichever address the loader chose.

Under run time binding, the same source code is again compiled into relocatable form, but this time no single binding step ever finalizes the addresses. Instead the MMU translates logical addresses into physical addresses continuously, access by access, while the program executes. The operating system could move this same running program from physical address 5000 to physical address 20000 in the middle of its execution, and the very next memory access would simply be translated against the new location, with the program never noticing anything happened.

{"headers":["Binding strategy","Physical address for this run","When it was fixed","Can it move mid execution"],"rows":[["Compile time","Always 5000, hardcoded directly into the compiled instructions","Before the program was ever compiled","No, never, a full recompile would be required"],["Load time","5000 this run, could be 20000 on a different run, but only one value once loaded","Once, by the loader, right before execution began","No, fixed for the rest of this run the moment loading finishes"],["Run time","Starts at 5000, later moved to 20000 by the operating system","Continuously, translated fresh on every access","Yes, freely, at any point while the process is running"]]}
8. Why Compile Time and Load Time Binding Still Matter
blocks.text: 8. Why Compile Time and Load Time Binding Still Matter

blocks.content: Given how completely run time binding dominates on modern systems, it is fair to ask why the other two are still worth learning at all. The answer is that they are not purely historical curiosities, they remain deliberate, sensible design choices in a specific and still common category of system: small embedded devices.

A simple embedded system, one that runs a single, permanently fixed program with no operating system multitasking multiple processes and no need to ever relocate anything, genuinely has nothing to gain from run time binding's extra per access translation overhead. In that narrow situation, choosing compile time or load time binding on purpose, deliberately trading away flexibility that will never be needed anyway, is often the simpler and cheaper engineering decision, not a mistake or an outdated leftover, and it remains a real, intentional choice on such devices today.
9. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle
A handful of misunderstandings around binding time come up repeatedly once this topic is put into practice, and they are worth calling out directly before moving on.

["Assuming every modern system always uses run time binding for absolutely everything, with no exceptions. A genuinely simple embedded system with a single permanently fixed program and no multitasking can still reasonably choose load time or even compile time binding on purpose, as a deliberate design decision rather than an oversight.","Confusing when addresses are decided with how addresses get translated. Binding time, compile time, load time, or run time, is a question about timing. The translation mechanism itself, such as paging or segmentation, is a related but genuinely separate question about structure. A system can use run time binding together with either mechanism, or with a simple base and limit register pair.","Believing load time binding is just as flexible as run time binding because it avoids the compile time restriction. Load time binding still permanently fixes the program's physical address the moment execution begins, it simply delays that fixing by one stage compared to compile time binding.","Forgetting that paging depends entirely on run time binding underneath it. Anyone who assumes paging could work with addresses fixed once at load time has missed why pages need to be relocatable and reloadable at any moment during execution."]
items: Assuming every modern system always uses run time binding for absolutely everything, with no exceptions. A genuinely simple embedded system with a single permanently fixed program and no multitasking can still reasonably choose load time or even compile time binding on purpose, as a deliberate design decision rather than an oversight.

Confusing when addresses are decided with how addresses get translated. Binding time, compile time, load time, or run time, is a question about timing. The translation mechanism itself, such as paging or segmentation, is a related but genuinely separate question about structure. A system can use run time binding together with either mechanism, or with a simple base and limit register pair.

Believing load time binding is just as flexible as run time binding because it avoids the compile time restriction. Load time binding still permanently fixes the program's physical address the moment execution begins, it simply delays that fixing by one stage compared to compile time binding.

Forgetting that paging depends entirely on run time binding underneath it. Anyone who assumes paging could work with addresses fixed once at load time has missed why pages need to be relocatable and reloadable at any moment during execution.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to name all three binding times cleanly: compile time, load time, and run time. Then be ready to explain precisely why only run time binding supports relocating a process after it has already started executing: because translation happens fresh on every single memory access rather than being fixed once, so the operating system only needs to update the mapping the MMU consults, not the process itself.

This timing question closes the loop opened in the Logical vs Physical Address chapter. Every mechanism explored later in the Memory Management module, paging, segmentation, and virtual memory, all assume run time binding is already in place underneath them, quietly making relocation and non contiguous placement possible on every single memory access.
